title: Minimum Operations to Make a Subsequence
statement:
You get an array `target` whose integers are all distinct and an integer array `arr` that may repeat values. A single operation places one integer of your choice anywhere in `arr`: at the front, at the back, or between two existing elements.

Return the fewest operations after which `target` appears as a subsequence of `arr`, meaning its elements can be found in `arr` in the same order, though not necessarily next to each other (other elements may sit between them).
constraints: All values in target are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Every element of `target` that is already in `arr` in the right order can be kept; everything else must be inserted. So the answer is `target.length` minus the longest common subsequence of the two arrays. A general LCS table costs O(n·m), far too slow for 10^5 by 10^5.

Because `target` has distinct values, each value names one position in `target`. Replace each useful element of `arr` by that position: a common subsequence is now exactly a strictly increasing run of positions, so the problem becomes a longest increasing subsequence, solvable in O(m log n).

## Approach

1. Build `position`, mapping each value of `target` to its index.
2. Walk `arr`; skip any `value` that is not in `target`, since it can never be matched.
3. Look up its `index`. Keep `tails`, where `tails[k]` is the smallest last index of any increasing run of length `k + 1` seen so far.
4. Binary search for the first slot with `tails[mid] >= index` and write `index` there (this extends `tails` when no slot qualifies).
5. `tails.length` is the longest kept run; return `target.length - tails.length`.

## Example 1, step by step

`target = [5, 1, 3]` gives `position = {5: 0, 1: 1, 3: 2}`. In `arr = [9, 4, 2, 3, 4]`, the values 9, 4 and 2 are not in `target` and are skipped. Value 3 has `index = 2`; `tails` is empty, so the search ends at `left = 0` and `tails = [2]`. The last 4 is skipped. One element can stay, so the answer is `3 - 1 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m log n): building the map is O(n) and each of the m elements of `arr` does one binary search over at most n tails.
- Space: O(n) for `position` and `tails`.

## Pitfalls

- The run must be strictly increasing: search for the first tail `>= index`, not `> index`, or a repeated value of `arr` would be counted twice.
- Values of `arr` missing from `target` must be skipped, not mapped to some default index.
- A full LCS table is correct but O(n·m) and times out at the limits.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `position` | map from a value of `target` to its index |
| `tails` | `tails[k]`: smallest ending index of an increasing run of length `k + 1` |
| `value` | current element of `arr` |
| `index` | position of `value` in `target` |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary search bounds over `tails` |
